topic: Banking - prompt caching + batch inference for cost optimization
question_text: A retail bank runs a GenAI application that generates personalized financial summaries for 2 million customers nightly. Each request shares a large, identical system prompt (~4,000 tokens of regulatory disclaimers and formatting rules) but has customer-specific data appended. The batch job runs overnight and is not latency-sensitive, but the bank wants to minimize Amazon Bedrock inference costs. Which combination of techniques will reduce cost the most?

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock prompt caching so the shared system prompt tokens are cached and billed at a reduced rate across requests.
Use Amazon Bedrock batch inference (CreateModelInvocationJob) to process the 2 million requests as an asynchronous batch at a lower per-token price than on-demand.
Provision the maximum Provisioned Throughput commitment to guarantee capacity for the nightly spike.
Route every request through Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing to always select the largest available model.
Send all 2 million requests concurrently through the synchronous InvokeModel API to finish as fast as possible.

explanation: Prompt caching (A) reduces the cost of the repeated 4,000-token system prompt by billing cached input tokens at a lower rate — ideal when a large prefix is identical across many requests. Batch inference (B) is designed for exactly this use case: large-volume, non-latency-sensitive workloads processed asynchronously at a discounted per-token price versus on-demand. Provisioned Throughput (C) is a fixed hourly commitment that is cost-effective only for sustained high-volume traffic, not a single nightly batch. Intelligent prompt routing to the largest model (D) increases cost. Synchronous concurrent InvokeModel (E) uses the most expensive pricing tier and risks throttling.
source_topic: Bedrock prompt caching, batch inference cost optimization, banking batch workloads

topic: Insurance - Provisioned Throughput vs on-demand scaling
question_text: An insurance company's claims chatbot uses Amazon Bedrock. Traffic is highly predictable: a steady, high volume of requests every business day from 08:00 to 18:00, and almost no traffic overnight or on weekends. During business hours the team frequently hits on-demand throttling limits. Which approach best balances reliable throughput and cost?

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a scheduled commitment aligned to business hours, and fall back to on-demand for any overflow.
Purchase a 6-month no-commitment Provisioned Throughput block and keep it running 24/7.
Stay entirely on-demand and implement client-side exponential backoff with retries to absorb all throttling.
Request a service quota increase to the maximum on-demand limit and disable all retry logic.

explanation: Provisioned Throughput guarantees a fixed inference capacity, eliminating on-demand throttling during the predictable business-hours peak, while scheduling the commitment to business hours (and using on-demand overflow) avoids paying for idle overnight/weekend capacity. Running Provisioned Throughput 24/7 (B) wastes money during the ~14 idle hours plus weekends. Pure on-demand with backoff (C) does not solve the throttling — it only delays requests, hurting the chatbot's responsiveness during peak. Maxing on-demand quota and disabling retries (D) still leaves requests subject to model-level throttling and removes resilience.
source_topic: Provisioned Throughput scheduling, on-demand throttling, predictable traffic cost optimization

topic: Journalism - model distillation for latency and cost
question_text: A news organization uses a large foundation model on Amazon Bedrock to auto-generate short headline suggestions. The quality is excellent, but per-headline latency and cost are too high for the real-time newsroom workflow. The team has thousands of high-quality headline examples produced by the large model. Which approach reduces latency and cost while preserving most of the quality?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation to fine-tune a smaller, faster model using the large model as the teacher and the collected examples as training data.
Increase the max_tokens parameter on the large model so fewer follow-up calls are needed.
Cache every generated headline in Amazon ElastiCache and serve identical cached headlines for all future articles.
Switch to Provisioned Throughput on the large model to lower the per-token price.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation transfers the capabilities of a large teacher model into a smaller, cheaper, lower-latency student model using teacher-generated training data — precisely matching this scenario (large model quality, need for speed/cost, abundant example data). Raising max_tokens (B) increases cost and latency. Caching (C) fails because headlines are article-specific and rarely repeat, so cache hit rate is near zero. Provisioned Throughput (D) may reduce per-token price but does not reduce the model's inherent per-request latency, which is the core problem.
source_topic: Bedrock Model Distillation, teacher-student, latency/cost optimization, journalism
